summary: Describes eight additional Diffie-Hellman groups for use in IETF protocols such as S/MIME, SSH, TLS and IKE, so implementers can share the same groups across protocols. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Two people can agree on a shared secret using public numbers called groups. This adds eight more ready-made sets of such numbers.

subtitle: Eight NIST-defined Diffie-Hellman groups, with test data and notes for using them in IKE, TLS, SSH and S/MIME.

tldr.problem: Different IETF security protocols each had their own scattered list of Diffie-Hellman groups, and the NIST groups had no RFC with parameters and test data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC publishes the parameters of three MODP groups and five elliptic curve (ECP) groups, test data for each, and instructions for using them in X.509, IKE, TLS, SSH and S/MIME.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can offer the same groups across protocols and verify their code against the test data.

today: RFC 5114 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated according to its metadata. It records the groups, test data and protocol notes as they stood in January 2008.

sections.title: Why More Groups
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman (D-H) key agreement needs agreed public parameters, called a group. RFC 5114 provides parameters and test data for eight D-H groups for protocols such as IKE, TLS, SSH and S/MIME, and for PKIX certificates that carry D-H keys. They complement earlier groups such as the Oakley groups of RFC 2409 and those in RFC 3526 and RFC 4492.

Three of the groups were already specified for IKE in RFC 4753 and five for TLS in RFC 4492, though the latter has no test data. The groups come from NIST publications and are defined with test data on a NIST web site, but had not yet been published in a formal NIST document at the time of writing. Putting them in one RFC is meant to help interoperability and FIPS validation.
sections.eli5: Many programs need to agree on a secret in public. This paper gathers eight approved recipes so they can all use the same ones.

sections.title: The Eight Groups
sections.content:
There are three standard prime-modulus (MODP) groups, each with a prime p, a generator g and a prime-order subgroup size q:

  • 1024-bit MODP group with a 160-bit prime order subgroup
  • 2048-bit MODP group with a 224-bit prime order subgroup
  • 2048-bit MODP group with a 256-bit prime order subgroup

There are five "random ECP" elliptic curve groups, of 192, 224, 256, 384 and 521 bits. Each is a curve y^2 = x^3 + ax + b (mod p) with its prime, parameters a and b, a generator point (gx, gy) and a group order n. The prime sizes are given in a compact form, for example p = 2^(521)-1 for the 521-bit group. The values are listed in hexadecimal in the RFC, and this explainer does not repeat them.

Appendix A gives test data for each group: for the MODP groups two parties' secret and public keys and the shared secret, and for the ECP groups the equivalent secret values and coordinates.
sections.eli5: Each group is a big public number recipe. Both people use the same recipe with their own private number, and end up with the same secret.

sections.title: Using the Groups in IETF Protocols
sections.content:
X.509: D-H public keys are represented as defined in RFC 3279, and if a KeyUsage extension is present the keyAgreement bits MUST be asserted.

IKE: MODP use is defined in RFC 4306 (IKEv2) and RFC 2409 (IKEv1). For the ECP groups, the key exchange payload format and shared key derivation of RFC 4753 MUST be used with both IKEv2 and IKEv1. Each group has an IKE transform ID.

TLS: MODP use is defined in TLS 1.1 and 1.0, and elliptic curves in RFC 4492. Five of the curves appear in the IANA EC Named Curve Registry under SECG names such as secp256r1.

SSH: RFC 4253 defined two MODP groups, while RFC 4419 lets MODP parameters be sent in key exchange messages, so no extra specification is needed for these groups. No RFC yet described elliptic curve D-H with SSH.

S/MIME: The sender takes the recipient's D-H parameters from the recipient's certificate, using CMS as in RFC 3852 and, for elliptic curves, RFC 3278.
sections.eli5: Each program already knows how to do the secret handshake. This paper just says which recipe names to plug in and where.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The strength of a derived key depends on the group, the size of the secret exponent and the entropy of the random number generator. The groups were chosen so that the work to solve the discrete logarithm problem is roughly comparable to an attack on the subgroup.

Secret key size matters. For MODP groups it should equal the size of q, and for elliptic curve groups it must equal the size of n. Larger secrets give no additional security, and smaller ones are likely to give dramatically less. The RFC gives an approximate equivalent strength per group, based on NIST recommendations: for example, the 256-bit ECP group is comparable to a 128-bit symmetric key and a 3072-bit RSA key.
sections.eli5: The secret number you pick has to be the right size, not too small and not bigger than needed. Too small and the secret is easy to guess.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content: IANA updated the IKE and IKEv2 registries to include five of the groups: the three MODP groups plus the 192-bit and 224-bit ECP groups. The other three ECP groups were already in the IKE registry. The registries list the groups by their Group Description, using the descriptions given in the RFC.
sections.eli5: The official list of group names and numbers was updated so everyone uses the same numbers for these groups.
